Mayor Helena Moreno Starts Initiative to Revamp Canal Street

Zoryn Johnson, Sports Editor
August 21, 2026
Sophia Renzi
Picture of Canal Street on August 8, 2026.
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:40
Instaread

During a press conference, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno announced her plans to revamp Canal Street, a popular staple of downtown New Orleans. 

On July 28, 2026, the Canal Street Renaissance Initiative was established by an executive order and is set to come in three phases including plans to support economic revitalization, draw in new investment, and boost the overall pedestrian experience. The initiative has already begun, focusing on “public safety, cleanliness, lighting, infrastructure, and quality of life,”according to the nola.gov website. 

“Canal Street is more than a roadway, it’s the front door to New Orleans and one of the most recognizable streets in America,” Moreno stated. “This initiative creates a clear strategy, strong accountability, and a dedicated coordinator within City Hall to ensure the work gets done to restore Canal Street as a vibrant destination for residents, businesses, and visitors,” Moreno added.

Alaila McMillian, a Loyola student majoring in psychology with a minor in communications expressed her concerns about the state of Canal Street.

“I believe that some areas need fixing, such as the sidewalks,” McMillian said.

Although her experience has been largely positive, she believes that the area could still see some improvement. 

“After reading the articles about Canal, I believe she [Mayor Helena Moreno] has the potential to improve Canal by supporting businesses and keeping the area clean,” McMillian added.

Shiloh El-Amin, an English Major from Slidell, Louisiana who currently lives in the city, shared their concerns with the street. 

“Personally, the biggest issues I’ve found with Canal Street are that the lighting makes it really hard for pedestrians at night, and the way the streetcar line isn’t exactly clean cut from main traffic [makes] it stressful for drivers, which ends up delaying the streetcar even more,” El-Amin explained.

The director of this initiative, Saydie Finkel, originally Mayor Moreno’s Chief of Staff, will oversee the plan’s execution and provide progress updates. 

“Canal Street is one of New Orleans greatest assets and one of the most iconic streets in our country. It has long been a place where commerce, culture, and community come together, and our goal is to ensure it once again reflects the energy and creativity that define our city,” Finkel stated.

Alaytia Nelson, a sophomore nursing major at Loyola, spoke on her experience with Canal Street. 

“It’s always been a place I love, so much to see, so much to do. My mom used to tell us stories about it, and over the years those stories have changed,” Nelson stated.

Although Nelson believes the current state of the famed New Orleans street is “alive and okay,” she also believes it no longer carries the same charm that it used to.

 “I believe a lot of Canal’s cultural identity has been taken over by capitalistic, forgettable shops that try to sell New Orleans rather than express or represent New Orleans,” Nelson said.  “My hope is for Canal Street to become more than a tourist attraction, a true representation of what New Orleans is: a city of culture, wonder, and history.” 

When asked about whether or not Mayor Moreno will deliver on the initiative, Nelson responded, “I believe she will. I’m choosing to look on the bright side — she has strong qualifications and shows real promise, so I have faith she’ll do her best for this city,” 

It has not yet been confirmed how long it will take to complete phase one of the Canal Street Renaissance Initiative, but the plan is already underway. Long-term goals include bringing in new businesses to occupy untenanted storefronts and expanding arts, entertainment, and cultural programming in the area. 

The Mayoral Staff has not responded for comment.
